title: Reformed disagree: some place faith subject in intellect alone (Molinaeus, Baron)
source_text: I. DE facultate cui fides inhaeret, & quae pro fidei subjecto habenda est, non idem sentiunt Doctores Reformati. Non desunt inter eos viri celeberrimi qui putant proprium fidei subjectum esse intellectum, non vero voluntatem. Nec enim ullum actum fidei tribuendum esse, qui non ab intellectu & mente eliciatur. Haec est sententia Petri Molinaei, ut manifeste colligitur ex Thesibus illius de Fide justificante, parte secunda, Thesi 18, & 19. Hanc quoque sententiam tenet Robertus Baronius in Philosophia Theologiae Ancillante: Fides, inquit, est in solo intellectu, proprie, subjective, & respectu suae essentiae. Exercit. 3. artic. 2. num. 5.
pass_a_gloss: Concerning the faculty in which faith inheres, and which is to be held as faith's subject, the Reformed Doctors do not think the same. There are not lacking among them most celebrated men who think the proper subject of faith is the intellect, not the will. For they hold that no act of faith is to be attributed which is not elicited by the intellect and mind. This is the opinion of Pierre du Moulin, as is clearly gathered from his Theses on Justifying Faith, part 2, theses 18 and 19. Robert Baron also holds this in Philosophia Theologiae Ancillans: Faith, he says, is in the intellect alone, properly, subjectively, and with respect to its essence (Exerc. 3 art. 2 n. 5).
pass_b_english: Reformed are not of one mind on which faculty is faith's subject.
Molinaeus and Baron place the proper subject in intellect alone: no faith-act not elicited by mind.

choices.why: Faculty seat of the habit/act, not 'topic'.
